Abstract

Partial discharge (PD) is the earliest measurable warning of insulation failure in high-voltage plants, yet on-site acoustic-emission (AE) measurements bury the diagnostic transients under non-stationary broadband, periodic and impulsive interference at signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) below −10 dB. Progress in deep learning denoising is fundamentally constrained by data scarcity: paired clean-noisy AE-PD recordings are physically impossible to obtain in the field, because the noise is intrinsic to the measurement. This work resolves the pairing problem with a hybrid protocol: a physics-based damped-oscillatory pulse generator supplies unlimited labelled clean signals spanning six discharge archetypes, while the real Q.Lin AE dataset anchors a grounded transfer benchmark. Composite substation noise (white Gaussian, magnetostrictive hum, powerline harmonics, narrowband interference and Bernoulli-Gaussian impulses) is injected into near-clean real windows so the original serves as ground truth. On this foundation, the work presents MR-TAE, a unified multi-task autoencoder coupling a multi-level wavelet-CNN encoder-decoder with a sequential BiGRU and 1-D Swin-Transformer bottleneck, attention-gated skips, and a dual-stream segmentation head that jointly denoises and localises PD events. The segmentation task acts as a morphology-preservation constraint that classical and single-task denoisers lack. Trained with Charbonnier, Focal and Generalised Dice losses under learned homoscedastic uncertainty weighting, the optimal configuration (NoMix curriculum) attains a mean synthetic normalised cross correlation (NCC) of 0.8282 and a 9.64 dB SNR improvement. At a −15 dB input, NCC of 0.378 is achieved compared to 0.158 for the strongest classical baseline (BayesShrink), representing a 2.4-fold margin of improvement. Furthermore, MR-TAE-NM also segments partial discharge types with a Dice score of 0.9192. On the grounded real transfer task, MR-TAE-FULL reaches an NCC of 0.4535 in a zero-shot setting and 0.7871 after Q.Lin domain adaptation, thereby exceeding the BayesShrink reference. Finally, LIME and SHAP analyses identify wavelet pooling and the multi-task head as the dominant contributors to low-SNR robustness. Removing the segmentation head collapses the real-domain NCC to -0.16, justifying its vital role in preserving the diagnostic pulse morphology.

Keywords: Partial Discharge, Signal Denoising, Wavelet CNN, Multi-task Learning.

Abstrak

Nyahcas separa (PD) merupakan amaran terawal yang boleh diukur bagi kegagalan penebat dalam loji voltan tinggi. Walau bagaimanapun, ukuran pancaran akustik (AE) di tapak menimbus fana diagnostik di bawah gangguan jalur lebar, berkala dan impulsif yang tidak pegun pada nisbah isyarat-kepada-hingar (SNR) di bawah -10 dB. Kemajuan dalam penyahhingaran pembelajaran mendalam secara asasnya dikekang oleh kekurangan data: rakaman AE-PD bersih-hingar yang berpasangan adalah mustahil secara fizikal untuk diperoleh di lapangan kerana hingar adalah intrinsik kepada pengukuran tersebut. Kerja ini menyelesaikan masalah pemadanan tersebut dengan satu protokol hibrid: sebuah penjana denyut ayunan redam berasaskan fizik membekalkan isyarat bersih berlabel tanpa had yang merangkumi enam arketip nyahcas, manakala set data AE Q.Lin sebenar menambat penanda aras pemindahan yang berasas. Hingar pencawang komposit (Gausan putih, dengung magnetostriktif, harmonik talian kuasa, gangguan jalur sempit dan impuls Bernoulli-Gausan) disuntik ke dalam tetingkap sebenar yang hampir bersih supaya isyarat asal berfungsi sebagai kebenaran asas. Berdasarkan asas ini, kajian ini membentangkan MR-TAE, iaitu sebuah pengekod auto pelbagai tugas disatukan yang menggabungkan pengekod-penyahkod CNN anak gelombang pelbagai aras dengan BiGRU jujukan dan leher botol Swin-Transformer 1-D, sambungan langkau berget perhatian, dan kepala pensegmenan dua strim yang berfungsi secara bersama untuk menyahhingar dan menyetempatkan kejadian PD. Tugas pensegmenan bertindak sebagai kekangan pemeliharaan morfologi yang tiada pada penyahhingar klasik dan tugasan tunggal. Dilatih dengan kerugian Charbonnier, Fokus dan Dadu Teritlak di bawah pemberat ketidakpastian homoskedastik yang dipelajari, konfigurasi optimum (kurikulum NoMix) mencapai min korelasi silang ternormal (NCC) sintetik sebanyak 0.8282 dan peningkatan SNR sebanyak 9.64 dB. Pada input -15 dB, NCC sebanyak 0.378 dicapai berbanding 0.158 untuk garis dasar klasik terkuat (BayesShrink), yang mewakili margin peningkatan sebanyak 2.4 kali ganda. Tambahan pula, MR-TAE-NM juga menyegmenkan jenis nyahcas separa dengan skor Dadu sebanyak 0.9192. Pada tugas pemindahan sebenar yang berasas, MR-TAE-FULL mencapai NCC sebanyak 0.4535 dalam tetapan sifar-sampel dan 0.7871 selepas penyesuaian domain Q.Lin, dengan itu mengatasi rujukan BayesShrink. Akhir sekali, analisis LIME dan SHAP mengenal pasti pengumpulan anak gelombang dan kepala pelbagai tugas sebagai penyumbang dominan kepada keteguhan SNR rendah. Penyingkiran kepala pensegmenan menjatuhkan NCC domain sebenar kepada -0.16, lantas mewajarkan peranan pentingnya dalam memelihara morfologi denyut diagnostik.

Kata Kunci: Nyahcas Separa, Penyahhingaran Isyarat, CNN, Pembelajaran Pelbagai Tugas.

# INTRODUCTION

## Background

In high-voltage electrical systems, insulation failures are a persistent source of equipment malfunction, unplanned outages, and costly maintenance. One of the primary causes is partial discharge (PD), a small self-extinguishing electrical breakdown that occurs within the insulation material before it fully bridges the gap. Although individual PD events may seem minor, their cumulative effect progressively weakens the insulation, eventually precipitating catastrophic failure.

Partial discharges produce brief transient signals that serve as the earliest measurable indicators of insulation degradation. In practice, however, these signals reach the sensor buried under interference from nearby equipment, environmental sources, and the measurement chain itself. When noise masks the PD signal, accurate detection and classification become unreliable, leading to delayed maintenance decisions and an elevated risk of serious insulation breakdown.

Traditional denoising techniques such as wavelet thresholding, Savitzky-Golay filtering, and Wiener filtering have long been applied to this problem. Their fundamental weakness is inflexibility: each method requires manual parameter tuning calibrated to a specific noise type, and a setting that works well under one condition will perform poorly under another. In addition, aggressive filtering distorts the very pulse morphology that downstream fault classification depends on, so a numerically clean output can still be diagnostically useless.

Recent advances in deep learning offer a more adaptive path. Convolutional neural networks and autoencoder architectures can learn noise patterns directly from data, removing the need for manual recalibration across noise conditions. Critically, they can be designed to preserve the morphological features of the PD pulse during denoising, ensuring the signal remains useful for fault-type identification. Traditional evaluation metrics such as SNR and MSE do not always reflect this diagnostic quality; a signal that scores well numerically may have lost the fine morphological features needed for classification. Morphology-sensitive metrics such as normalised cross-correlation, combined with discharge-type classification accuracy, provide a more complete picture of whether denoising has genuinely succeeded.

## Problem Statements

The The accurate analysis of PD signals is the cornerstone of condition-based maintenance for high-voltage assets including power transformers, underground cables, and gas-insulated switchgear. PD is the earliest measurable precursor of insulation degradation, preceding catastrophic failure by months to years. The diagnostic value of a PD measurement lies not merely in its detection, but in its morphology: the amplitude, rise time, oscillation frequency, and decay envelope of the pulse collectively carry the signature of the underlying discharge type, whether corona, surface discharge, internal void, or electrical treeing, each of which demands a different maintenance response.

The central challenge of on-site PD monitoring is that these morphological features are routinely destroyed before they can be read. Acoustic-emission sensing is the preferred field-deployable modality because its piezoelectric transducers mount non-intrusively on the outside of the equipment enclosure, galvanically isolated from the high-voltage circuit, and capture PD-induced ultrasonic pressure transients across the 20 to 500 kHz band. In a live substation or energised cable tunnel, however, this measurement is simultaneously contaminated by at least five co-present interference sources: broadband thermal and electronic noise from the sensor and acquisition chain; magnetostrictive core-lamination vibration at 100 Hz and its harmonics; electromagnetic coupling of the 50 Hz powerline fundamental and its third harmonic at 150 Hz; narrowband interference near 80 kHz from communications equipment and switch-mode power supplies; and sparse high-amplitude impulsive transients from switching operations, whose sub-microsecond rise times closely mimic a genuine PD pulse. Field signal-to-noise ratios below negative 10 dB are routine, and in the worst case the diagnostic pulse is completely buried.

Classical denoising methods are structurally unequal to this composite noise field for three reasons. First, wavelet thresholding, Savitzky-Golay filtering, and Wiener filtering each require the a priori selection of a mother wavelet, window length, or spectral model tuned to one specific noise statistic; a threshold calibrated for corona PD will fail on internal PD, and no single setting is optimal across the full composite field. Second, all three are linear or quasi-linear operators, fundamentally incapable of separating impulsive interference whose time-domain morphology overlaps that of a genuine PD pulse. Third, aggressive coefficient suppression removes the high-frequency detail that encodes the diagnostic signature, so improved noise figures can coincide with lost diagnostic content.

A deeper challenge is the absence of suitable training data. Paired clean and noisy recordings of the same PD event cannot be physically obtained in the field, because the composite noise is intrinsic to any energised high-voltage measurement. This data-scarcity constraint forces any supervised learning approach to first resolve the pairing problem before training can begin, and it means that real-world datasets suitable for evaluation are extremely rare, making generalisation from laboratory conditions to field deployment an open research question.

Existing deep learning denoisers address the manual-tuning and linearity limitations but leave the remaining gaps unresolved. Most are trained on short synthetic windows containing only one to three isolated pulses, evaluated under simplified single-component noise, and assessed solely by MSE or SNR improvement, metrics that reward amplitude smoothing without any guarantee that the diagnostic pulse morphology has been retained. A persistent gap therefore remains between reported benchmark figures and practical field applicability, and closing it requires a training data strategy that resolves the clean-noisy pairing problem, a noise model faithful to real substation conditions, and an evaluation protocol that directly measures morphological recovery rather than inferring it from energy ratios.

## Objectives

**a)** To implement state-of-the-art conventional PD denoising methods on both synthetic and real acoustic-emission PD signals to serve as performance benchmarks.

**b)** To develop a deep learning-based denoising model trained on synthetic and real-world AE-PD signals, evaluated against a composite noise field spanning −15 dB to +15 dB across five co-present interference types.

**c)** To analyse denoising performance using both traditional signal-quality metrics and a morphology-sensitive evaluation protocol to verify that diagnostic pulse features are preserved after denoising.

# Literature review

This chapter presents a comprehensive review of previous research on various techniques and theories related to partial discharge denoising methods. It further examines the challenges and constraints related to applying PD denoising methods and discusses how the proposed approach tackles these challenges. Additionally, a comprehensive analysis of the Machine Learning architectures of the proposed denoising method in existing literature will be provided, comparing it with similar approaches and highlighting its advantages and limitations.

## Partial Discharge

Partial discharge (PD) is a significant phenomenon that serves as an early indicator of insulation degradation in electrical systems. Recent studies have focused on understanding the characteristics of PD signals and their implications for insulation breakdown, particularly in high-voltage equipment.

Recent research has highlighted the critical role of PD in assessing the reliability of electrical insulation. Salem et al. (2022) conducted an experimental investigation into leakage current characteristics, demonstrating that monitoring these currents can provide insights into the reliability of insulators. Their findings suggest that leakage currents are closely linked to PD activity, indicating that effective monitoring can preemptively identify insulation issues before catastrophic failures occur. This is consistent with the work of Chan et al. (2023), who reviewed various PD localization techniques, emphasizing the necessity of continuous monitoring to prevent insulation breakdown.

The relationship between PD and insulation materials has also been explored in recent studies. For instance, Liu et al. (2024) utilized a Fabry-Pérot optical fiber sensor array to localize dual PD in transformer windings, showcasing the effectiveness of optical 6 methods in detecting PD signals. This approach is particularly relevant as it provides a non-invasive means of monitoring insulation integrity, which is crucial for maintaining the reliability of transformers. Additionally, the study by Qian (2024) analyzed the correlation between GIS PD current waveforms and charge quantities, further elucidating how PD characteristics can inform about the state of insulation in gas-insulated switchgear.

Moreover, the implications of PD for insulation breakdown have been underscored by the work of Fang and Hu (2024), who proposed a hybrid particle swarm optimization method for PD signal denoising. Their research indicates that effective denoising techniques can enhance the clarity of PD signals, allowing for more accurate assessments of insulation condition. This is particularly important as PD signals are often contaminated by noise, which can obscure critical information regarding insulation health.

In summary, the recent literature emphasizes the importance of partial discharge as a key indicator of insulation degradation. The integration of advanced monitoring techniques, such as optical sensors and sophisticated signal processing algorithms, has the potential to significantly enhance the reliability of electrical systems. Continued research in this area is essential for developing effective strategies to mitigate the risks associated with insulation breakdown.

## Types of Partial Discharge

Partial Discharge (PD) signals manifest in several distinct forms depending on their origin and location within high-voltage insulation systems. The primary types include internal discharges, surface discharges, and corona discharges. Internal discharges occur within voids or cavities of solid insulation materials, producing characteristic pulse 7 patterns with short rise times and relatively high amplitudes. These signals typically exhibit frequencies ranging from a few MHz to several hundred MHz.

Surface discharges develop along insulation boundaries or interfaces between different dielectric materials. These discharges generate signals with broader pulse widths and more irregular occurrence patterns compared to internal discharges. The frequency spectrum of surface discharge signals typically spans from hundreds of kHz to tens of MHz, with distinctive phase relationships to the applied voltage.

Corona discharges occur in regions of high electric field stress around sharp edges or protrusions in gas-insulated systems. These signals are characterized by their repetitive nature and strong correlation with the polarity of the applied voltage. Corona discharge pulses typically exhibit lower amplitudes than internal discharges but maintain a more consistent pattern of occurrence.

## Types of Interference

The identification and detection of partial discharge (PD) signals can be challenging due to different types of interference, such as white noise, periodic narrowband interference, and additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN). Each type of noise brings its own difficulties, making it important to apply specific techniques to filter them out and improve the clarity of PD signals.

White noise consists of random signals that contain equal power across all frequencies. In the context of PD signal detection, white noise can obscure low-amplitude PD signals, making it challenging to distinguish them from background noise. This type of interference is prevalent due to thermal noise and electronic components in high-voltage environments.

Periodic narrowband interference comes from external sources like power-line harmonics or electromagnetic coupling. This type of interference shows up in specific frequency ranges and often overlaps with PD signals, making it harder to separate the signal from the noise. Unlike white noise, periodic narrowband interference follows a predictable pattern, which makes it easier to tackle using frequency-based methods.

Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) is a type of noise that follows Gaussian distribution and adds random variations to the PD signal. It is commonly found in communication and electronic systems and becomes especially problematic when the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is low. This kind of noise can make PD signals appear faint or distorted.

## Artificial Intelligence in Partial Discharge Denoising

Deep learning has become a transformative technology in various fields, including signal processing and fault diagnosis. When it comes to partial discharge (PD) signal denoising, deep learning methods are particularly effective at removing noise while preserving critical features associated with PD signal.

Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with multiple layers, often referred to as deep architectures, to model complex patterns in data. These networks can automatically learn detailed features from raw data, making them powerful for tasks involving large amounts of data, such as images, audio, or time series signals. For PD signal denoising, the model can be trained on pairs of noisy and clean signals, enabling it to learn the mapping between the two. These networks can automatically learn detailed features from raw data, making them powerful for tasks involving large amounts of data, such as images, audio, or time-series signals.

Kumar et al. Kumar (2023) introduces a wavelet kernel-aided deep learning framework specifically designed for denoising PD signals. This method combines wavelet transforms with deep learning architectures to enhance the denoising process by leveraging the strengths of both techniques. The wavelet transform decomposes the signal into different frequency components, allowing the deep learning model to focus on relevant features while effectively suppressing noise.

Furthermore, the research by Dong et al. (2023) highlights the use of generative adversarial networks (GANs) for data augmentation in scenarios with unbalanced and small sample sizes. This approach can significantly enhance the training datasets available for deep learning models, thereby improving their robustness and accuracy in denoising and classifying PD signals. The primary advantage of deep learning approaches in PD denoising is their ability to automatically learn relevant features from raw data without manual feature extraction. This helps improve performance, especially in noisy environments where traditional methods may not work as well.

However, deep learning models require large amounts of labelled training data to achieve optimal performance, which can be a limitation in some situations where it's hard to gather enough labeled samples. Additionally, these models are often computationally demanding and may require significant resources for both training and running the models.

### Model Architecture

The evolution of deep learning architectures for signal denoising and reconstruction has progressed significantly from simple Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to sophisticated hybrid models. Early implementations, such as those by P. Liu et al. (2019) demonstrated that combining Deep CNNs with Multilevel Wavelet Decomposition could effectively handle biomedical signal noise by leveraging the frequency-domain sparsity of wavelet coefficients. This concept was further advanced by Faúndez Quezada et al. (2024), who proposed the Multi-Level Wavelet Convolutional Neural Network (MWCNN) to condition extremely noisy industrial signals.

However, traditional CNNs suffer from a limited local receptive field, which restricts their ability to model long-range dependencies in time-series data. To address the complexity of stochastic non-stationary noise, modern architectures have shifted toward integrating mechanisms that capture global context and temporal dynamics simultaneously.

#### Swin Transformer

To overcome the locality constraints of CNNs, attention mechanisms were introduced to allow networks to weigh the importance of different input features dynamically. O. Oktay et al. (2018) pioneered medical imaging with the Attention U-Net, which utilized gating signals to suppress irrelevant background noise. Building upon this, the Swin Transformer, introduced by Z Liu et al. (2021), represents a paradigm shift in processing hierarchical features.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 2.1: Swin Transformer Model Architecture

Unlike standard Transformers, which calculate self-attention globally which lead to quadratic computational complexity, the Swin Transformer computes self-attention within non-overlapping local windows. It then utilizes a Shifted Window mechanism to allow for cross-window connections, enabling the model to capture global long-range dependencies with linear computational complexity.

In the context of denoising, this hierarchical structure is critical. As noted by Wei et al. (2018), multi-scale feature fusion is essential for distinguishing between signal details and noise artifacts. The Swin Transformer achieves this by progressively merging image patches (or signal segments) in deeper layers, creating a hierarchical representation that understands the semantic shape of the Partial Discharge pulse rather than just local pixel intensity. This ability to model global context is superior to standard CNNs for recovering morphological features in low-SNR environments.

#### Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU)

While Transformers excel at spatial and global context, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) remain the gold standard for modelling sequential temporal dynamics. Specifically, the Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) has proven highly effective for time series prediction and reconstruction.

According to Mingda et al. (2025), the BiGRU improves upon standard RNNs and LSTMs by utilizing two parallel layers: one processing the sequence forward and the other backward. This bidirectional processing ensures that the reconstruction of a specific time step is informed by both past and future contexts, which is vital for accurately determining the onset and decay of transient pulses.

![The structure of BiGRU | Download Scientific Diagram](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 2.2: Bi-GRU Architecture

The integration of such dynamic selection mechanisms into denoising frameworks was explored by Wang et al. (2020). They proposed a wavelet dynamic selection network, 12 demonstrating that adaptive temporal filtering can significantly enhance noise suppression performance. Furthermore, Mingda et al. (2025) highlighted the efficacy of dual-stream deep learning architectures, suggesting that combining spatial feature extractors with temporal sequence modelers results in a robust system capable of handling complex time-series classification and reconstruction tasks. By creating a bottleneck that fuses these two streams, the model can leverage the BiGRU to capture the temporal evolution of the PD signal while the Transformer handles global morphological consistency.

#### 1-Dimesnional U-Net

A critical limitation of the standard U-Net is the passive nature of its skip connections. In a standard setup, features from the noisy encoder are concatenated directly with the decoder. As noted by K. G. (2020), this sequential paradigm can lead to a fallacy where noise is reintroduced into the reconstruction path, forcing the decoder to filter out artifacts that were explicitly passed to it.

To resolve this, O. Oktay et al. (2018) introduced the concept of Attention Gates (AGs) in their seminal work on Attention U-Net. Although originally applied to pancreas segmentation, the mechanism is highly relevant to PD denoising. The Attention Gate uses deeper, coarser feature maps which contain global context to generate a gating signal. This signal acts as a filter for the skip connections, highlighting salient features while suppressing irrelevant regions (background noise).

This mechanism ensures that the skip connections are active and selective. By incorporating soft attention, the model learns to focus computational resources on the target signal, significantly reducing false positives in the reconstruction. This approach aligns with the findings of Mingda (2025), who emphasized that multi-scale feature fusion must be selective to avoid noise propagation in image and signal denoising tasks.

#### Multi-Level Wavelet Convolutional Neural Network

While U-Nets excel at structural recovery, standard pooling layers (MaxPooling) result in irreversible information loss, particularly regarding high-frequency details. To mitigate this, recent research has integrated Discrete Wavelet Transforms (DWT) directly into the neural network architecture.

![Multi-level wavelet-CNN architecture. It consists of two parts: the... |  Download Scientific Diagram](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 2.3: Multi-Level Wavelet CNN Architecture

P. Liu et al. (2019) proposed Deep CNNs with Multilevel Wavelet Decomposition, demonstrating that replacing pooling layers with DWT allows the network to downsample data without losing information. The DWT separates the signal into frequency sub-bands, approximation and detail coefficients, all of which are fed into the network. This preserves the spectral integrity of the signal, which is often lost in standard downsampling.

Building on this, Faúndez Quezada et al. (2024) developed the Multi-Level Wavelet Convolutional Neural Network (MWCNN) specifically for conditioning extremely noisy industrial signals. Their architecture utilizes the DWT for downsampling and the Inverse DWT (IDWT) for upsampling. This ensures the process is mathematically lossless. The feature map dimensions are reduced, but the total information content is preserved in channel dimensions.

This wavelet-integrated approach is particularly effective for non-stationary signals like Partial Discharge. As highlighted by Wang et al. (2020) in their work on wavelet 14 dynamic selection networks, the ability to process signal features in the frequency domain allows the model to distinguish between the broadband signature of stochastic noise and the specific spectral footprint of the fault signal, leading to superior denoising performance compared to pure time-domain CNNs.

### Training Methodology

The efficacy of deep learning models in processing non-stationary time-series data is heavily dependent on the training strategy employed. Recent literature suggests that training a model solely on a single objective often leads to suboptimal generalization, particularly when the target signal is sparse and the noise is overwhelming. To address this, this research integrates three advanced pedagogical strategies: Multi-Task Learning, Curricular Training, and Adaptive Loss Weighting.

#### Multi-Task Learning (MTL)

Multi-Task Learning is a training paradigm that aims to leverage useful information contained in multiple related tasks to improve the generalization performance of all the tasks. As defined by Zhang & Yang (2018), MTL mimics human learning by transferring knowledge across domains. For instance, learning to recognize the shape of an object helps in classifying it.

In the context of deep neural networks, Ruder (2017) categorizes MTL architectures into soft and hard parameter sharing. Hard parameter sharing, which is utilized in this research, forces the network to learn a unified latent representation that is robust enough to support multiple downstream objectives.

For Partial Discharge (PD) analysis, Hiton et al. (2021) demonstrated that solving auxiliary tasks (such as classification) alongside the primary task (denoising) acts as a powerful regularizer. By forcing the shared encoder to extract features that are 15 semantically meaningful for classification. The model is less likely to overfit the noise patterns in the denoising task. This aligns with the findings of Kendall et al. (2018), who showed that multi-task systems often outperform single-task models because the auxiliary tasks provide inductive bias, guiding the model to prefer solutions that are structurally valid rather than just minimizing pixel error.

#### Curricular Training

Training deep networks on data with low Signal-to-Noise Ratios (SNR) is notoriously difficult due to the cold start problem, the model struggles to find any gradient direction when the signal is buried in noise. Bengio et al. (2009) introduced Curriculum Learning to solve this by organizing training examples in a meaningful order of increasing difficulty, like how humans learn simple concepts before complex ones.

In the domain of noise suppression, Braun et al. (2017) proposed a curriculum strategy where the model is first exposed to high-SNR samples where the signal structure is clear. Once the model learns the fundamental morphology of the waveform, the noise level is progressively increased. Higuchi et al. (2021) further validated this dynamic curriculum approach for keyword spotting in noisy environments, showing that it prevents the model from converging to local minima where it simply outputs zero to minimize the average error.

For PD signals, this approach is critical. A study by Wang et al. (2019) on varying SNR levels showed that models trained via curriculum learning achieved faster convergence and higher final accuracy than those trained on a randomized mix of SNRs, as the initial easy examples allowed the network to learn the critical rise-time and decay features of the PD pulse before being challenged by heavy interference.

#### Loss Function

The choice of loss function determines how the network penalizes errors. Standard Mean Squared Error (MSE) is often insufficient for signal reconstruction because it is sensitive to outliers and tends to produce blurry outputs To improve reconstruction fidelity, Lai et al. (2017) proposed the Charbonnier Loss for image super-resolution. Unlike MSE, which squares the error by heavily penalizing large outliers but neglecting small textures, Charbonnier loss creates a more balanced penalty. Siegel & Chapman (2021) applied this to CT-scan denoising, finding that it preserved soft tissue textures significantly better than MSE. In PD signals, this translates to better preservation of the high-frequency oscillating tails of the pulse.

PD signals are inherently imbalanced. Lin et al. (2017) introduced Focal Loss to address this foreground-background imbalance in object detection. By adding a modulating factor to the standard cross-entropy loss, Focal Loss down-weights the contribution of background noises and focuses the model's attention on hard, misclassified PD Pulses. Su et al. (2025) recently demonstrated that Adaptive Focal Loss is superior for keypoint detection in time-series data where the target event is sparse.

Combining regression and classification losses requires balancing weights. Arbitrarily setting these is often suboptimal. Kendall et al. (2018) proposed a principled method using Homoscedastic Uncertainty to automatically learn these weights during training. This formulation allows the model to dynamically trust one task more than the other based on the learned noise variance (𝜎𝜎), ensuring that the easier task does not dominate the gradient updates.

## Traditional Partial Discharge Denoising Methods

### Wavelet transforms

Wavelet transform is a simple yet powerful method for cleaning partial discharge (PD) signals, especially useful when the noise in the signal's changes over time. It works by breaking a signal into smaller parts across different scales, which makes it easier to separate unwanted noise from important details. This process, called multi-resolution analysis, allows for a detailed examination of both the time and frequency aspects of a signal.

The method uses a wavelet function, a small wave-like pattern to analyze the signal. By adjusting the size and position of the wavelet, the transform captures details at different levels. The result is a set of coefficients that show how much of the signal matches each wavelet. High-frequency noise, usually represented by small coefficients, can be reduced or removed through a process called thresholding. The cleaned signal is then reconstructed, retaining its essential features while minimizing noise.

![](data:image/x-emf;base64,)

Figure 2.4: Block diagram of wavelet denoising technique

He and Ni (2023) introduced a denoising method for PD signals that applies wavelet transform to separate the noise from the desired signal. Their approach demonstrated that wavelet transform is highly effective in dealing with time-varying noise, an important characteristic of PD signals, by adapting to different frequencies present in the signal. This makes wavelet transform a valuable tool for improving the clarity of PD signals in various applications.

Sornsen, Suppitaksakul, and Kitpaiboontawee (2021) applied wavelet transform to PD signals from generators, showing how this method improves the signal quality even in noisy environments. Their study reinforced the importance of wavelet transform in enhancing the detection and analysis of partial discharge events, highlighting its applicability in real-world electrical systems.

Shams, Anis, and El-Shahat (2021) focused on using wavelet transform to denoise heavily contaminated PD signals in high-voltage cables. Their work demonstrated how wavelet transform, particularly discrete wavelet transform (DWT), can be used to filter out noise without losing important signal features, making it effective in harsh environments with significant signal interference.

In conclusion, wavelet transform is an effective method for denoising PD signals, capable of handling varying noise levels while preserving critical signal features. Its ability to operate in both time and frequency domains makes it an ideal tool for improving the quality of PD signals in electrical power systems. Future studies could explore how to optimize wavelet selection for specific types of PD signals and real-time applications

#### Wavelet families

Wavelet families are fundamental components of wavelet theory, providing the basis for various applications in signal processing, image analysis, and data compression. Each wavelet family possesses unique properties that make them suitable for specific tasks, influencing the performance of both the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) and Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT). Understanding these families is crucial for selecting the appropriate wavelet for a given application.

##### Daubechies

Daubechies wavelets, developed by Ingrid Daubechies, are among the most widely used wavelet families. They are characterized by their compact support and orthogonality, which allows for efficient signal representation. The Daubechies wavelets are denoted as dbN, where N represents the order of the wavelet. Higher-order Daubechies wavelets provide better approximation properties but require more computational resources.

![](data:image/x-emf;base64,)

Figure 2.5: Daubechies wavelets family

##### Haar

Haar wavelets represent the simplest form of wavelet functions and serve as a foundational example of wavelet theory. They are characterized by their discontinuous nature and compact support, making them computationally efficient but less effective for smooth signals. Despite their simplicity, Haar wavelets are still used in basic applications where rapid computation is essential.

![](data:image/x-emf;base64,)

Figure 2.6: Haar Wavelet Family

The selection of an appropriate wavelet family is crucial for optimizing denoising performance in partial discharge signal analysis. Each family offers distinct advantages depending on the characteristics of the input signal and the specific requirements of the task at hand either noise suppression, feature preservation, or computational efficiency.

##### Symlets

Symlets are a modification of Daubechies wavelets designed to be nearly symmetric, which minimizes phase distortion in signal reconstruction. This property makes Symlets particularly useful in applications requiring high fidelity in signal representation. Research indicates that Symlet wavelets perform well in various contexts, including biomedical signal processing and image compression.

![](data:image/x-emf;base64,)

Figure 2.7: Symlets Wavelet Family

##### Coiflets

Coiflets are another family of wavelets characterized by their smoothness and symmetry. They possess additional moments equal to zero, which enhances their performance in certain applications. Coiflets are particularly advantageous when preserving signal features is essential, such as in denoising tasks. Studies have highlighted their effectiveness in both Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) and Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) frameworks, showcasing their adaptability across various domains.
