Consider a clean window with signal variance (after peak normalisation the variance is of order this magnitude) and a raw composite-noise window with . The current SNR is . To realise a target of −10 dB, the scale factor is , so the noise is multiplied by ≈6.31 before addition, raising its variance to and bringing the SNR to . This illustrates how the _severity_ of corruption is set independently of its _character_: the same composite recipe is simply scaled to each of the seven target levels.

## Artificial Intelligence (AI) Denoising Model Architecture

### Convolutional Neural Network

The first architecture established a baseline using a sequential Pure CNN design comprised of six consecutive convolutional blocks. The model accepts input data shaped as 2048 X 1 X 1, with kernels and strides padded appropriately to accommodate the data dimensions. Inside each of the six blocks, the processing begins with a convolutional layer featuring 36 filters, utilizing a kernel size of 19 X 1 and a stride of 1X1 with zero padding. This is immediately followed by a batch normalization layer and a ReLU activation layer to introduce non-linearity. The block concludes with an average pooling layer configured with a 2 X 1 size and a stride of 4 X1 without padding. Upon exiting the final convolutional block, the feature maps undergo a flattening process before passing through a fully connected layer with 2,048 units. Finally, the data is reshaped back to the original 2048 X 1 X 1 dimensions to complete the signal reconstruction.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 3.6: Pure CNN Architecture

### Modified 1D U-Net

The second model adapts the classic 1D U-Net architecture, a structure traditionally employed in 2D image denoising and segmentation, to feature a symmetrical encoder-decoder arrangement with skip connections. Designed specifically for signal processing, the network utilizes standard convolutional layers for feature extraction and max-pooling for downsampling. The encoder section is composed of four blocks with progressively increasing depth,64, 128, 256, and 512 filters, while the bottleneck contains two convolutional layers, each holding 1024 filters. Following the bottleneck, the decoder mirrors the encoder with four blocks decreasing in filter size from 512 down to 64. Throughout the network, convolution operations utilize a kernel size of 3 X 1 with zero padding and ReLU activation, while downsampling is achieved via max-pooling with a pool size and stride of 2 X 1 at the end of each encoder block. To recover spatial resolution, the decoder employs transposed convolutions for upsampling, using a kernel and stride of 2 X 1 with zero padding. Crucially, the architecture integrates skip connections that copy and crop feature maps from the encoder blocks to concatenate them with the corresponding upsampled maps in the decoder, pairing half of the upsampled features with the encoded ones. The reconstruction is finalized by a single 1 X 1 convolutional kernel that reduces the dimensionality to 2,048, matching the original input signal.

\`![Refer to caption](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 3.7: Modified 1D U-Net

### Multi-Level Wavelet Convolutional Neural Network (MWCNN)

The third model, the Multi-Level Wavelet-CNN (MWCNN), was implemented to address the information loss inherent in standard pooling layers by replacing them with the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT). Utilizing the WaveTF library for efficient GPU processing within TensorFlow, this backbone performs downsampling by splitting signals into frequency sub-bands and upsampling via the Inverse Discrete Wavelet Transform (IDWT), using the Haar mother wavelet to ensure mathematically lossless feature extraction. The encoding path consists of three blocks: the first contains three 64-filter convolutional layers, while the subsequent two blocks follow a specific pattern where a 2n-filter layer is followed by three n-filter layers (with n=128 and 256, respectively). A DWT operation concludes each encoding block. The central bottleneck is constructed from eight convolutional layers: a starting layer of 1024 filters, followed by six layers of 512 filters, and a closing layer of 1024 filters. The decoding phase comprises two blocks initiated by IDWT operations. The first decoding block processes features through three 256-filter layers and one 512-filter layer before a second IDWT, while the second decoding block contains three 64-filter layers without skip connections. All convolutional layers employ a kernel size of 3, a stride of 1, and ReLU activation, with zero padding applied in the decoding stages. Rather than a third decoding block, the model concludes with a flatten layer feeding into two dense layers of 128 and 256 neurons (ReLU activated), ending with a final linear dense layer of 2,048 units to match the input length.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 3.8: Multi-Level Wavelet Convolutional Neural Network (MWCNN) Architecture

## MR-TAE Architecture

MR-TAE is a **single** encoder-bottleneck-decoder autoencoder with two output heads. Every model studied in this report: every ablation row, the linear and IDWT decoders, the loss variants: is this one architecture with specific components enabled or disabled, or with a specific upsampling operator selected. This chapter describes the architecture component-by-component with exact tensor shapes and then explains how the ablation configurations and the decoder variation are obtained by toggling within it. Figure 2 is the corresponding block diagram.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

### Overview and data flow

The model maps a noisy input window to a denoised waveform and a per-sample segmentation logit tensor . The forward path is:

The encoder progressively halves temporal resolution while doubling channels; the bottleneck models temporal and global context at the most compressed scale; the decoder reverses the encoder, re-injecting the skip features through attention gates; and the two heads produce the denoised signal and the PD-event mask.

### Input projection

The single-channel input is first lifted to the base channel width by a 1-D convolution with kernel size 7 and padding 3:

_input<sub>proj</sub>_: Conv1d(1 → 32,kernel=7,padding=3),(B,1,2048) → (B,32,2048).

The wide kernel gives the first layer a 7-sample receptive field, enough to begin responding to short pulse edges before any downsampling.

### MWCNN encoder (db4-DWT)

#### Per-level structure: Conv-first, then DWT

Each of the three encoder levels applies **two** Conv-BatchNorm-GELU blocks and then a **Daubechies-4 DWT** downsampling step. Crucially, the **skip connection is taken from the post-Conv, pre-DWT** features, so the skip retains full temporal resolution at that level. The DWT splits the signal into a low-frequency (approximation) and a high-frequency (detail) sub-band, each at half length, and stacks them along the channel dimension: so the channel count doubles while the length halves.

#### The DWT layer

The DWT is implemented as a fixed (non-trainable) grouped 1-D convolution with the db4 decomposition filters. For an input of length L, the signal is reflect-padded, convolved separately with the low-pass and high-pass db4 filters, downsampled by 2, and the two results concatenated on the channel axis. The db4 wavelet (8 filter taps) is chosen because its asymmetry and support match the asymmetric, fast-rising PD pulse better than the symmetric Haar wavelet.

#### Mathematical form of the DWT

Let and be the db4 low-pass (decomposition) and high-pass (decomposition) filters, each of length 8. For a single-channel signal , one DWT level computes the approximation and detail sub-bands by filtering and decimating by two:

where is reflect-padded at the boundaries. The layer stacks along the channel axis, so a input Because the db4 filters form a perfect-reconstruction quadrature-mirror pair, no information is lost: the original can be recovered exactly by the inverse transform (below). This is the precise sense in which DWT downsampling is _lossless_, in contrast to max- or average-pooling, which are many-to-one and therefore irreversible.

The db4 decomposition low-pass coefficients are approximately  
with the high-pass filter obtained by the usual alternating-flip relation. The eight-tap support gives the filter enough vanishing moments (db4 has four) to represent the smooth portions of the signal compactly while concentrating the pulse edges in the detail band.

#### Mathematical form of the IDWT

The inverse transform reconstructs from using the reconstruction filters and :

In the layer, this is implemented by zero-insertion upsampling (placing the sub-band samples at even indices), reflect padding, convolution with and , and summation of the two contributions. This is followed by a deterministic crop and pad to the stored target length. A input becomes and is then cropped. This IDWT layer is exactly the operator used by the IDWT decoder variation.

#### Tensor shapes

With base channel widths \[32, 64, 128\] and an input length of 2048, the encoder produces:

Table 3.3: Encoder tensor dimensionalities at each level of the discrete wavelet transform.

| Level | Conv output (skip)    | After db4 DWT |
| ----- | --------------------- | ------------- |
| 1     | skip₁ = (B, 32, 2048) | (B, 64, 1025) |
| 2     | skip₂ = (B, 64, 1025) | (B, 128, 513) |
| 3     | skip₃ = (B, 128, 513) | (B, 256, 257) |

The slight departure from exact halving (1025 rather than 1024, etc.) is a deterministic consequence of the db4 filter length and the reflect padding and is handled exactly in the decoder by storing each level's skip length and cropping/padding to match. The final encoder output is

#### The plain-encoder ablation

When wavelet pooling is disabled (the MR-TAE-noWavelet and UNet-BiGRU-Swin configurations), the MWCNN encoder is replaced by a **standard convolutional encoder** that uses Conv-BatchNorm-GELU blocks followed by max-pooling for downsampling, with the same channel progression and the same skip interface. This isolates the contribution of frequency-aware wavelet sampling versus conventional pooling.

### Pre-bottleneck projection

A 1×1 convolution maps the encoder output channels to the bottleneck width (256), giving the canonical bottleneck tensor on which all bottleneck variants operate.

### BiGRU and Swin-1D (sequential)

The full bottleneck (the Hybrid Bottleneck) processes the representation through a bidirectional GRU and then a 1-D Swin Transformer, wrapped in a residual connection. The arrangement is **sequential**: the BiGRU output is the Swin input: so local temporal context is established first and refined by global attention.

#### BiGRU

A 1×1 convolution projects to the GRU input width; a **2-layer bidirectional GRU** with **128 hidden units per direction** (256 total) processes the sequence along the time axis, in both forward and backward directions. The BiGRU captures the local temporal signature of a PD pulse: a fast rise followed by oscillatory decay: and its surrounding context, which helps distinguish a genuine pulse (preceded by a quiet region) from an impulsive artefact.

##### GRU recurrence

For each direction, a GRU cell updates its hidden state from the input and the previous state through an update gate a reset gate , and a candidate state This update mechanism is formalized by the following sequence of operations:

The bidirectional layer runs one such recurrence left-to-right and another right-to-left and concatenates their hidden states, so each output step is conditioned on the entire window. Stacking two layers lets the second layer model higher-order temporal dependencies on the first layer's representation. The gating is what allows the GRU to retain the memory of a quiet pre-pulse region across many time steps without the vanishing-gradient pathology of a vanilla RNN.

#### Swin-1D

The BiGRU output is projected to the Swin embedding dimension (256) and processed by a **1-D Swin Transformer** of depth 2 with 8 attention heads and window size 32. Attention is computed within non-overlapping windows of 32 time steps for linear complexity; alternate blocks apply a **shifted window** (cyclic roll by half the window) so that information flows across window boundaries. A relative-position bias is added within each window. Window-stationary properties of the noise (a hum frequency, an impulsive pattern that recurs across the window) are exactly the kind of global structure this block can model.

##### Windowed self-attention

The 257-step sequence is partitioned into non-overlapping windows of steps (with padding to a multiple of W). Within each window, multi-head self-attention is computed:

where are linear projections of the window's tokens, are the per-head dimension, and is a learnable **relative-position bias** indexed by the pairwise offset of tokens within the window. Restricting attention to a window reduces the cost from (full attention) to i.e. linear in sequence length. To let information cross window boundaries, alternate Swin blocks apply a **shifted window**: the sequence is cyclically rolled by before partitioning and rolled back afterwards, so tokens that were on opposite sides of a boundary share a window in the next block. Each block wraps attention and a two-layer GELU MLP (hidden ratio 4) in pre-norm residual connections:

With depth 2, the block contains one regular-window and one shifted-window stage, which together give every token an effective receptive field spanning the whole 257-step bottleneck.

#### Residual wrapping and bottleneck ablations

A residual projection adds the bottleneck input to the processed output, stabilising training. The bottleneck has four ablation forms, selected by the use_bigru/use_swin flags:

- **BiGRU + Swin** (full): sequential, as above;
- **BiGRU only**: Swin removed;
- **Swin only**: BiGRU removed;
- **Conv only**: both removed, replaced by two residual conv blocks (the minimal bottleneck used when both sequence models are disabled).

These four forms underpin the bottleneck rows of the ablation grid.

### Attention-gated skip connections

Each decoder level fuses the corresponding encoder skip through an **attention gate** before concatenation. The gate computes, from the decoder (gating) feature g and the encoder skip x,

In this mathematical formulation, , , and denote convolutions, and represents the logistic sigmoid activation function. The gate computes a per-location attention coefficient . This coefficient functions to suppress skip activations dominated by noise while emphasizing specific spatial features aligned with the emerging reconstruction of the decoder. A residual configuration can also be employed to retain the original skip connection alongside the gated output. When attention gates are disabled within the architecture, the raw skip connection is concatenated directly without this filtering mechanism.

#### Why gate the skip at all

In a plain U-Net, the encoder skip is concatenated to the decoder feature unchanged. This is a double-edged sword for denoising: the skip carries the full-resolution detail the decoder needs, but at low SNR that same skip is dominated by noise, so concatenating it raw reintroduces precisely the contamination the bottleneck just suppressed. The attention gate resolves this tension by letting the decoder's own (already partly denoised) feature act as a query that scores each location of the skip: locations consistent with the emerging reconstruction are passed through while locations dominated by noise are attenuated (). The gate is additive and uses an intermediate channel width that keeps its parameter overhead small relative to the conv blocks. The noAttn ablation directly measures whether this selective gating helps or whether the raw skip suffices.

### The decoder and the IDWT variation

#### Per-level structure

The decoder mirrors the encoder over three levels. At each level the feature map is **upsampled ×2**, concatenated with the (gated) skip of matching length, and refined by two Conv-BatchNorm-GELU blocks. The channel progression is \[128, 64, 32\], ending at 32 channels and full length 2048. Each level is told the exact target length (the stored encoder skip length), so the boundary-induced length offsets are resolved deterministically by cropping/padding the upsampled feature to match the skip.

#### The decoder variation: linear vs IDWT

Upsampling is the single controlled **decoder variation**:

- **Linear variant (use_idwt = False)** This employs an upsampling operation with a scale factor of 2 utilizing linear interpolation. This is followed by convolution, batch normalization, and a GELU activation. This interpolation-based upsampling produces outputs mathematically proximate to the input, functioning as a conservative denoising operation.
- **IDWT variant (use_idwt = True).** A Daubechies 4 (db4) Inverse Discrete Wavelet Transform (IDWT) reconstructs the higher-resolution feature map from the stacked low-pass and high-pass sub-bands. This is achieved through zero-insertion upsampling, reflect padding, convolution with the db4 reconstruction filters, and the subsequent summation of the low-pass and high-pass contributions. A deterministic crop and pad operation then ensures the tensor matches the target sequence length. The IDWT performs a highly aggressive and frequency-aware reconstruction that can diverge significantly from noisy input.

Both variants share **all** other weights and structure. IDWT is therefore not a separate model but a different upsampling operator inside the one MR-TAE. This framing is what allows any linear-vs-IDWT difference to be attributed cleanly to the reconstruction operator.

#### A note on loading the IDWT variant

The IDWT variant is only architecturally consistent if the use_idwt flag is set when the model is instantiated. Where a checkpoint's training-time configuration omits this flag, it must be inferred (from the model identifier, the registry, or the presence of IDWT-specific weights in the state dictionary) before loading, and the loaded model must pass a positive grounded-NCC sanity check. This loading correctness is a prerequisite for the IDWT rows of the results to be meaningful; it is part of the benchmark integrity work that precedes result filling.

### Output heads

#### Reconstruction head

A 1-D convolution maps the decoder's 32-channel, full-length features to a single output channel with **no activation** (linear output), because the denoised AE signal is bipolar:

#### Segmentation head (dual-stream fusion)

The segmentation head is a **dual-stream fusion** module that combines the global bottleneck features with the local decoder features to produce per-sample class logits over the five classes {background, corona, surface, internal, treeing}:

Fusing a global stream with a local stream allows the segmenter to be both context-aware and temporally precise. The global bottleneck representation captures window-level context, while the full-resolution decoder features localize events exactly. When multi-task learning is disabled in specific ablation configurations, the segmentation head is omitted. This renders the model a strict denoising autoencoder.

### How the model becomes each configuration

Every model studied is this architecture with a specific flag set. The flags are:

| **Flag**            | **Effect when enabled**                                |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| use_wavelet_pooling | MWCNN db4 encoder/decoder (else plain conv + max-pool) |
| use_bigru           | BiGRU in the bottleneck                                |
| use_swin            | Swin-1D in the bottleneck                              |
| use_attention_gates | attention-gated skips (else raw skips)                 |
| use_mtl             | dual-stream segmentation head (else denoise-only)      |
| use_idwt            | IDWT decoder upsampling (else linear)                  |
| loss_config         | A, B or C                                              |

The 13-configuration ablation, the decoder variation, and the loss variants represent distinct coordinates within this hyperparameter space. This design ensures a strictly controlled comparative analysis. Each evaluated model diverges from the full architecture exclusively along the toggled dimensions. Parameter counts naturally scale with the enabled structural components. The Swin block and the BiGRU sequence introduce the highest parameter overheads. Locked parameter counts are documented per configuration for transparency.

### Design alternatives and why they were not chosen

Several alternative design choices were available at each stage; documenting them clarifies the rationale for the architecture and frames the ablation.

- **Pooling vs DWT.** Max/average pooling and strided convolution are the conventional downsamplers, but all three are lossy in the high-frequency band that defines a PD pulse. DWT was chosen for its lossless, invertible, frequency-splitting behaviour; noWavelet ablation quantifies the cost of maxpooling.
- **Parallel vs sequential bottleneck.** The BiGRU and Swin could be arranged in parallel (concatenating their outputs) or sequentially. The sequential arrangement (BiGRU → Swin) was chosen so that the recurrent layer first establishes local temporal context, which the attention layer then refines globally; this mirrors the intuition that global reasoning is most useful once local structure is available.
- **Transformer vs Swin.** A full self-attention transformer would model all pairwise interactions but at quadratic cost; the windowed Swin variant restores linear complexity while the shifted-window mechanism preserves cross-window flow: a better fit for a 257-step bottleneck on a single consumer GPU.
- **Linear vs IDWT upsampling.** Rather than commit to one upsampler, both are retained as a controlled decoder variation, so the choice is settled empirically under the unified protocol rather than by assertion.
- **Fixed vs learned loss weights.** Fixed multi-task weights are brittle as the curriculum changes the relative task difficulty; homoscedastic-uncertainty weighting was chosen to adapt the balance automatically.

## Curriculum and Losses

This chapter describes how MR-TAE is trained: the three-phase noise curriculum (and the phased/no-phase/NoMix variations), the three loss configurations and their mathematics, the optimisation settings, and the training infrastructure that makes long, multi-model runs robust. The training data are generated fresh each epoch, so the model never sees the same noisy realisation twice.

### The three-phase curriculum

Exposing the model directly to −15 dB composite noise from the first epoch is unstable: when the pulse is invisible the reconstruction gradient is near-random and training can collapse. Curriculum learning resolves this by presenting easy examples first and increasing difficulty gradually, so the model learns clean PD structure before it must extract it from extreme noise.

#### Phase schedule

The curriculum has three phases of increasing difficulty, each defined by an SNR range and a noise type:

| **Phase**  | **SNR range** | **Noise type**                  | **Purpose**                                   |
| ---------- | ------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| 1 (easy)   | +5 to +15 dB  | WGN only                        | Learn clean PD pulse structure                |
| 2 (medium) | −5 to +5 dB   | WGN + impulsive                 | Handle moderate noise and impulsive artefacts |
| 3 (hard)   | −20 to −5 dB  | Composite (all five components) | Master extreme, realistic noise               |

Within each phase the SNR for each training window is sampled uniformly from the phase range, and the noise type is the phase's type. The phase boundaries are defined by epoch counts; the scheduler maps each absolute epoch to a (phase, SNR range, noise type) tuple. Per-phase epoch counts are configuration-dependent and reported as Phase 1: 20; Phase 2: 30; Phase 3: 50 with a total of 100 epochs.

#### Curriculum variations (phased, no-phase, NoMix)

The curriculum is itself a **training variation** of the one model:

- **Phased**: the three-phase schedule above, applied in sequence.
- **No-phase**: the model is trained directly on the full composite distribution across the entire SNR range, with no easy-to-hard progression. The phased-vs-no-phase comparison quantifies the value of the curriculum for low-SNR robustness.
- **NoMix (trained: recommended).** The same three-phase schedule but **without mixed-type augmentation windows**: each training window contains a single discharge archetype only. This forces purer per-class morphology learning and is the **best configuration overall**: mean synthetic NCC **0.8282**, NCC @ −15 dB **0.3777**, SNR improvement **9.64 dB**, Dice **0.9192**, grounded real NCC **0.4535** (+17.9% over BayesShrink 0.3844, no fine-tuning). Parameters: 3.05 M; latency: 17.1 ms (batch 1).

### Loss configurations

Three supervision regimes are studied on the _same_ architecture, isolating the effect of the loss from the effect of the architecture. The reconstruction term is common to all three; the segmentation term and the task-balancing differ.

#### Reconstruction loss (): Charbonnier Loss

The reconstruction term is the **Charbonnier loss**, a smooth, robust approximation to the L1 norm:

Where is clean signal, is denoised output, is small constant for numerical stability.

Charbonnier is preferred over MSE because PD pulses are spiky: an L2 loss would over-penalise the large-amplitude pulse samples and under-penalise the noise floor, biasing the denoiser toward over-smoothing. Charbonnier's near-L1 behaviour away from zero makes it robust to the high-amplitude impulsive outliers that contaminate the signal.

#### Segmentation losses: Focal and Generalized Dice

PD signals are highly **imbalanced**: e.g., a 20 µs signal may contain a pulse for only 1 µs (~5% positive, 95% background). Using standard **Cross-Entropy Loss** would bias predictions toward Background. Two complementary losses address this:

- **Focal loss**

down-weights well-classified background samples and concentrates learning on hard examples (pulse boundaries, impulsive artefacts):

**Generalized Dice loss (GDL)** weights each class inversely to its frequency, so the rare PD classes are not swamped by the background:

**Generalized Dice Loss (GDL) Nomenclature**

- : The scalar loss value representing the optimization objective to minimize the discrepancy between the predicted segmentation and the true class distributions.
- : The class index differentiating the distinct label categories, such as the dominant background noise and the highly localized partial discharge events.
- : The frequency-balancing weight assigned to class , computed as the inverse square of the total class volume to ensure that misclassifications in rare data subsets heavily influence the gradient update.
- : The continuous probability array generated by the neural network for class .
- : The binary ground truth target array designating the actual presence of class .
- : The mathematical intersection of the predicted and true sets, representing the correctly classified true positive instances for the respective class.
- : The summation of all elements within the target array for class , representing the total true volume of that specific class within the sample.

#### Task balancing: homoscedastic uncertainty

When both heads are active, their losses are balanced automatically by **homoscedastic-uncertainty weighting**: each task carries a learnable log-variance , and the combined loss is

The term prevents the model from trivially inflating to ignore a task. As training proceeds, the weights adapt across curriculum phases: early on the reconstruction term dominates, while later both terms matter. The σ parameters are part of the optimiser state and are saved in checkpoints.

#### Derivation

The weighting follows from maximising the joint Gaussian likelihood of the two task outputs. Modelling each task as a Gaussian with observation noise , the negative log-likelihood of the combined model is

Identifying with the task loss gives exactly the weighted objective above (up to the constant that lets us learn directly for numerical stability). The interpretation is intuitive: a task with large irreducible uncertainty is automatically down-weighted (its coefficient shrinks), while the penalty stops the optimiser from declaring every task maximally uncertain. This removes the brittle manual coefficient that a naïve objective would require, and: importantly for this work: lets the balance drift correctly as the curriculum makes the reconstruction task progressively harder.

#### The three configurations

| **Config**   | **Reconstruction** | **Segmentation**            | **Task balancing**                |
| ------------ | ------------------ | --------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| **A** (full) | Charbonnier        | Focal + Generalized Dice    | Learned homoscedastic uncertainty |
| **B**        | Charbonnier        | Generalized Dice (no Focal) | Learned homoscedastic uncertainty |
| **C**        | Charbonnier + SSIM | (no segmentation head)      | Single-task (no MTL)              |

Config A is the most heavily supervised; Config B simplifies the segmentation supervision; Config C is reconstruction-only with an added 1-D SSIM term that rewards local structural similarity. The comparison of A/B/C on the full model isolates the effect of loss design on both synthetic quality and real-domain transfer.

### Optimisation

Training uses the AdamW optimiser (learning rate 3e-04, weight decay 1e-04) with a cosine-annealing schedule and a short linear warm-up, gradient clipping at max-norm 1.0 (important for stabilising the BiGRU under extreme-noise gradients), and automatic mixed precision (FP16 forward, FP32 master weights) for throughput and memory efficiency. The data seed is fixed for reproducibility. Batch size is selected per model from its parameter count to leave GPU-memory headroom, but usually at 32.

### Training infrastructure and resilience

Long multi-model training runs are made robust by several mechanisms: atomic per-epoch persistence of the full training state (so a kill never corrupts the session), checkpoint-based resume (model, optimiser, scheduler, loss σ, AMP scaler and history), automatic batch-size halving on CUDA out-of-memory, a thermal monitor that pauses training above a temperature threshold, and dynamic early stopping based on a rolling improvement rate. These do not affect the trained model's definition but ensure that the reported checkpoints are the product of complete, recoverable runs. Any model that was halted at a partial epoch is flagged with its epoch/phase for transparency in the metrics record.

### Checkpoint selection

For a fair comparison, each model's evaluated checkpoint is selected by an identical, stable procedure rather than by a single noisy validation point. Across the last few late-epoch checkpoints of a model, the winner is the one with the highest **mean NCC across all seven SNR levels** of the frozen synthetic sweep (with the −15 dB NCC as a tie-break). The selected checkpoint and the selection record are stored per model, so the same procedure and the same frozen test sets are applied to every configuration.

Because the candidate set, the scoring metric (mean NCC over the seven-level sweep), the tie-break (−15 dB) and the frozen test sets are identical for every model, the comparison is fair by construction: no model benefits from a luckier validation point or an easier curriculum phase than another.

## Experimental Setup and Reproducibility

This chapter specifies the datasets, the test-set freezing procedure, the hardware, and the controls that make the experiment reproducible. The overriding principle is that every model is measured under _identical_ conditions, so that performance differences are attributable to the model alone.

### Datasets and splits

Two evaluation datasets are used, both frozen before any benchmarking:

- **Synthetic AE-PD test set.** Generated from the six archetypes A-F with the composite noise model, at 2000 windows per SNR level across (−15 to +15 dB), giving 14000 windows. Each window carries a clean reference and a per-sample class mask, enabling NCC, RMSE, SNR-improvement, Dice and FPR.
- **Real Q.Lin grounded test set.** Clean Q.Lin windows (held-out split) with composite noise injected at the seven SNR levels (−15 to +15 dB), at 5000 windows per SNR level, giving 35 000 noisy evaluation rows (5000 clean references × 7 SNRs). The clean window is the NCC reference.

The real corpus is split deterministically (seed-fixed) into a held-out test split and a small pool; the grounded set is built from the test split so that no window used for noise-pool purposes leaks into evaluation.

### Freezing and hashing

Both test sets are written to disk once and **SHA-256 hashed**; the hashes are recorded in the reproducibility appendix (Appendix D). Any change to a test set changes its hash, so the integrity of the evaluation data is auditable. The hashes are ade2b9ec7b61681153ed475ef329b50e2524fa6f3426ae5314b10481b4bc9561, 16ce0d927a11e1e47201df8f82822a4f20d6ff119a1091486c74f510dbcb0658, 6eb400e41464415fb3da8bba3b01a492879ad0c8bb2b87ce0e610cbac5fcbcb2, 42640d8e4a4c9e14570203dfa6e7e83658bea28f6714d7b40e941b1093732e64.

### Unified evaluation protocol

Every trained configuration is evaluated on its selected checkpoint, and every classical baseline on the same frozen sets, through one evaluation pipeline that computes the full metric set. The protocol is identical across entries:

1\. Run the model on the frozen synthetic set; compute NCC, RMSE, SNR-improvement, Dice, FPR, and per-SNR NCC.

2\. Run the model on the frozen real grounded set; compute the grounded NCC overall and per SNR.

3\. Measure inference latency (batch 1 and batch 32, CUDA-synchronised) and count parameters.

For very large, grounded sets, a frozen, seed-fixed subset of rows is used so that all models are evaluated on the same rows.

### Hardware and software

Experiments run on a single consumer GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4070, 12 GB) with CUDA and automatic mixed precision. The software stack is PyTorch with NumPy/SciPy for signal processing and PyWavelets for the classical wavelet baseline. Per-model latency is locked in paper/metrics_master.json.

### Benchmark integrity gates

The re-locked benchmark (2026-05-31) applied sanity gates before accepting results: grounded real NCC must be non-negative (except documented failure modes such as noMTL); synthetic per-SNR sweeps must be monotone-plausible; and IDWT checkpoints must load with use_idwt=true verified. All models in the headline tables passed these gates.

## Baselines and Evaluation Metrics

### Traditional Partial Discharge Denoising Method

Three classical denoisers anchor the learned models, all evaluated under the identical protocol. None of the classical methods has a segmentation capability, so Dice and FPR are reported as not applicable for them. Their parameter count is zero and their latency is measured on CPU.

#### Wiener filtering

The Wiener filter is an optimal linear filter under a local stationarity assumption and is frequently included as a classical reference in signal denoising. Unlike heuristic thresholding methods, the Wiener filter computes a statistical estimate of the unknown signal by minimizing the Mean Square Error (MSE) between the estimated and actual uncorrupted signals. It is highly effective when the spectral characteristics of both the underlying signal and the background noise can be reliably estimated.

- 1. **Principle of Operation**

The underlying premise of the Wiener filter assumes that the observed signal is a linear combination of the true signal and additive noise. In the discrete time domain, the observation model is defined as:

Where is the observed noisy signal, is the true unknown signal, and is the additive noise component. The objective of the Wiener filter is to design a linear system with an impulse response that produces an estimate minimizing the expected value of the squared error:

When operating in the frequency domain and assuming the signal and noise are uncorrelated random processes, the optimal filter transfer function is derived as

Where represents the Power Spectral Density (PSD) of the clean signal and represents the Power Spectral Density of the noise.

- 1. **Estimation of Power Spectral Densities**

In practical applications involving transient phenomena like partial discharge, the exact PSD of the clean signal is unavailable prior to filtering. The filter must be implemented adaptively using empirical estimates. The noise PSD is typically estimated from signal-free segments of the captured waveform or from baseline background measurements.

The PSD of the observed signal is calculated directly from the input data. Because the signal and noise are assumed to be uncorrelated, their relationship is additive in the power domain:

Consequently, the unknown signal PSD can be approximated by subtracting the estimated noise PSD from the observed PSD:

The maximum function is utilized to enforce numerical stability and prevent negative power estimates caused by local statistical fluctuations in the frequency domain.

- 1. **Filtering and Reconstruction**

Once the transfer function is constructed, the filtering operation is executed strictly in the frequency domain. The Fourier transform of the observed signal is multiplied by the calculated Wiener filter frequency response:

This formulation acts as a frequency-dependent scaling factor. If the signal power is significantly larger than the noise power at a specific frequency, approaches 1, preserving the component. If the noise dominates, approaches 0, heavily attenuating the component. Finally, the denoised time-domain signal is reconstructed by applying the Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) to the modified spectrum .

#### BayesShrink Algorithm

While standard soft thresholding relies on a fixed or universal threshold, the BayesShrink algorithm offers a data-driven, adaptive approach. It determines the optimal threshold for each wavelet subband by minimizing the Bayesian Risk, assuming a Gaussian prior for the signal coefficients. This makes it particularly effective for PD signals where noise levels may vary across different frequency scales.

The BayesShrink method operates on the assumption that the wavelet coefficients in each detail subband are a mixture of signal and noise. The observation model is defined as:

Where _Y_ represents the observed noisy wavelet coefficients, _X_ represents the unknown noise-free signal coefficients and _V represents the noise component_

- 1. **Estimation of Noise Variance**

The first step is to estimate the noise variance (\\sigma^2) present in the signal. Since the noise typically dominates the high-frequency components, the noise variance is robustly estimated from the first decomposition level (HH_1 subband) using the Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) estimator:

where are the coefficients in the finest detail subband. The factor 0.6745 rescales the MAD to be a consistent estimator for the standard deviation of a normal distribution.

- 1. **Estimation of Signal Variance**

For each subband, the variance of the observed coefficients (\\sigma_Y^2) is calculated as:

where is the number of coefficients in that subband. The variance of the signal () is then derived by subtracting the noise variance from the observed variance:

- 1. **Threshold Calculation**

The optimal threshold () for each subband is computed adaptively based on the estimated signal and noise characteristics. The threshold is defined as:

This formulation ensures that if the signal variance () is large, indicating strong PD activity, the threshold is small, preserving the signal. Conversely, if the signal variance is small, indicating mostly noise, the threshold becomes large, aggressively suppressing the coefficients.

- **Soft Thresholding and Reconstruction**

Once the unique threshold is calculated for each detail subband, Soft Thresholding is applied to the coefficients _Y_:

Finally, the denoised signal is reconstructed using the Inverse Discrete Wavelet Transform (IDWT) with the modified coefficients. This adaptive nature makes BayesShrink generally superior to VisuShrink for PD signals, as it minimizes the loss of signal energy in subbands where the PD pulse is dominant.

#### Savitzky Golay Filtering

Unlike Wavelet methods which operate in the frequency domain, the Savitzky-Golay (SG) filter is a time-domain smoothing technique based on local least-squares polynomial approximation. It is particularly effective for preserving the shape and height of waveform peaks while reducing random high-frequency noise.

- **Principle of Operation**

The SG filter works by sliding a window of fixed size (2*m*+1) across the digital signal. Within each window, a polynomial of order _p_ is fitted to the data points using the method of linear least squares. The central point of the window is then replaced by the value of the fitted polynomial at that position.

The denoised value at point _i_ is given by a weighted sum of the adjacent data points:

_x_ is the input filter, _m_ is the window size (_N_ \= 2*m* + 1), _c<sub>j</sub>_ are the convolution coefficients derived from the least-squares fit of the polynomial.

- **Parametric Selection**

The performance of the SG filter in PD denoising is highly sensitive to two key parameters. A larger window smooths out more noise but may flatten narrow PD pulses. A window (_N_) that is too small will fail to remove noise effectively. A higher-order polynomial (_p_) follows the signal variations more closely, preserving sharper peaks (high frequency) but also passing more noise. A lower order provides smoother results but may distort the pulse amplitude.

In this study, the parameters are optimized to balance the trade-off between noise suppression (improving SNR) and morphological preservation (maintaining pulse rise-time). The SG filter is often used as a final smoothing stage or a baseline comparison for time-domain filtering efficiency.

### Metric definitions

#### Mean Square Error (MSE)

The average squared difference between the original and denoised signal amplitudes. It Focuses on **pixel-perfect reconstruction**.

Where is amplitude of clean signal at point , is amplitude of denoised signal at point , while is the total number of samples The lower MSE, the more the denoised signal closely matches the original waveform.

#### Root Mean Square Error (RMSE)

The square root of MSE. Brings error back to the **same unit as the signal** (Volts or Amperes), making it more interpretable.

It helps to understand the **average magnitude of residual distortion** in the signal.

#### Signal to Noise Ratio (SNR)

The ratio of **clean signal power** to the **residual noise power** in the denoised signal.

Where numerator () means energy of the clean signal and denominator (): energy of residual noise

SNR is the industry-standard metric. When the SNR is strong, it affirms that PD pulse is **much stronger than remaining noise**. **Input SNR** and **Output SNR** to compute SNR improvement.

#### Normalized Cross Correlation (NCC)

NCC measure the similarity in **shape and phase** between the clean and denoised signals, **regardless of amplitude**.

**The range** of NCC is **\[-1:1\],** where equals perfectly inverse, is no correlation and means identical. It is critical because the **shape of the pulse** (rise/decay times) indicates **fault type**. A model can have low MSE but poor NCC if it **blurs sharp PD peaks**.

#### Dice coefficient and false-positive rate (FPR)

For the segmentation head, **Dice** measures the overlap between predicted PD-event samples (foreground = any non-background class) and the true mask:

**FPR** is the fraction of true-background samples predicted as PD: a key field metric because impulsive noise tends to induce false PD detections.

#### Efficiency

**Parameter count** (millions) and **inference latency** (milliseconds, batch 1 and batch 32, CUDA-synchronised) characterise the deployment cost.

#### Grounded real Q.Lin NCC: headline transfer metric

The grounded real metric is the NCC between the model's output and the _clean_ Q.Lin window, when the input is that window plus injected composite noise. Unlike the older input-referenced NCC (which merely measures how close the output is to the noisy input, and is maximised by doing nothing), the grounded NCC measures genuine denoising quality on real signals: a perfect denoiser scores 1.0, and a model that destroys the real pulse morphology scores low even if it suppresses noise. It is reported overall and per SNR.

# Results

This chapter presents a comprehensive evaluation of the MR-TAE architecture across four interlocking axes: (i) a 13-configuration component ablation study that cleanly isolates each module's contribution; (ii) a wider training-variation and baseline comparison spanning curriculum schedules, decoder choices, deep-learning competitors, and classical signal-processing methods; (iii) SNR-sweep performance from −15 dB to +15 dB capturing the model's robustness across the full noise spectrum; and (iv) real-domain transfer to unseen Q.Lin recordings, with and without domain-adaptive fine-tuning. Explainability analyses via LIME by Ribeiro et al. (2016) and SHAP by Lundberg and Lee (2017) corroborate the quantitative findings with input-attribution evidence. Throughout, the grounded real-domain NCC (gNCC) computed against the Q.Lin dataset serves as the headline real-world metric, as it imposes the most stringent test of morphological generalisation beyond the synthetic training distribution.

Wavelet pooling and the MTL head are the two most critical components. The noMTL result is particularly instructive: removing the segmentation head collapses grounded real NCC from 0.4366 to −0.1605, a full sign reversal confirming that the segmentation constraint is a morphology-preservation forcing function essential for real-world transfer.

The reference configuration, MR-TAE-FULL, achieves a synthetic NCC of 0.7991, a grounded real-domain NCC of 0.4366, an SNR improvement of 7.01 dB, and a Dice score of 0.9015 for discharge-type segmentation. The ranked NCC drops relative to MR-TAE-FULL are: noWavelet (−0.1688), noMTL (−0.1509), noBiGRU (−0.1427), noSwin (−0.1359), and noAttn (−0.1223). The wavelet pooling stage and the multi-task learning (MTL) segmentation head emerge as the two most critical components by this ranking.

### Wavelet Pooling (noWavelet)

Removing the wavelet-domain encoder produces the single largest performance degradation, reducing synthetic NCC by 0.1688 and collapsing the grounded real NCC from 0.4366 to −0.0337, a sign reversal that indicates the denoised output is anti-correlated with the morphological ground truth. The result confirms that lossless frequency decomposition is irreplaceable: conventional strided convolution or max-pooling discard the high-frequency sub-bands that encode the sharp rise-time and oscillatory decay characteristics of PD transients. Without wavelet pooling, the decoder has no frequency-resolved representation from which to reconstruct these diagnostically critical features.

### Multi-Task Learning Head (noMTL)

Removing the segmentation head collapses the grounded real-domain NCC from 0.4366 to −0.1605, the most severe real-world regression in the entire ablation. This full sign reversal, implying that the model's output is morphologically opposed to the ground truth, confirms that the MTL head acts as a morphology-preservation forcing function. By compelling the shared encoder to produce representations that are simultaneously sufficient for both denoising reconstruction and discharge-type discrimination, the segmentation auxiliary objective prevents the encoder from collapsing to a global smoothing solution that scores well on synthetic SNR metrics but fails to reproduce pulse geometry in real recordings.

### Bidirectional GRU (noBiGRU)

Without the BiGRU recurrent module, synthetic NCC falls by 0.1427 to 0.6564 and the NCC at −15 dB deteriorates to 0.0585, a near-total loss of pulse recovery at extreme noise. The BiGRU provides the model with access to long-range temporal context in both causal directions, which is essential for correctly estimating the smooth exponential decay tail of PD pulses that extends many hundreds of samples beyond the initial rising edge. Loss of this sequential modelling forces the decoder to rely entirely on local convolutional features, which are insufficient for reconstructing temporally extended transients buried in broadband noise.

### Swin Transformer (noSwin)

Removing the Swin Transformer bottleneck reduces synthetic NCC by 0.1359 and lowers gNCC by 0.1079. The shifted-window attention mechanism provides global receptive field coverage within the bottleneck, enabling the model to relate widely separated pulse instances within a window and to exploit the quasi-periodic repetition structure of PD events. Its removal forces the architecture to rely solely on the BiGRU for global context, which is effective for sequential continuity but less capable of modelling non-adjacent pulse interactions simultaneously.

### Attention Gate (noAttn)

Removal of the attention gates on the skip connections yields a NCC drop of 0.1223 and reduces gNCC substantially to 0.1014, the lowest among the single-component removals. The attention gate suppresses noise-contaminated feature maps in the skip pathways before they reach the decoder; without gating, corrupted encoder activations are passed directly to the decoder, degrading the quality of the reconstructed signal even if the bottleneck representation is well-formed.

### Compound and Loss-Variant Configurations

The noSwin-noBiGRU configuration achieves NCC 0.7974 and gNCC 0.4365 essentially matching MR-TAE-FULL, revealing that Swin and BiGRU are substantially redundant when both are absent, as each compensates for the other's global-context role. The noSwin-noAttn configuration achieves NCC 0.7998 and gNCC 0.4171, confirming again that the wavelet pooling and MTL head are the load-bearing components. In contrast, noBiGRU-noAttn is catastrophic (NCC 0.5536, gNCC 0.0180), showing that the combination of sequential and skip-path degradation removes essential structural information.

The loss-variant configurations illustrate that balanced loss formulation is critical. FULL-LossB (which increases the reconstruction weight relative to the segmentation term) achieves a competitive gNCC of 0.4551 but reduces SNR improvement to 1.71 dB and degrades synthetic NCC to 0.6270, indicating over-emphasis on morphological fidelity at the expense of noise suppression. FULL-LossC (which reduces the segmentation weight) collapses gNCC to 0.1699, corroborating the MTL head's centrality.

### Curriculum and Decoder Variants

Among the MR-TAE family, the NoMix curriculum variant (MR-TAE-FULL-NM) achieves the highest synthetic NCC of 0.8282 and SNR improvement of 9.64 dB, establishing it as the primary recommended configuration for synthetic-domain deployment. The NoMix curriculum withholds the hardest mixed-noise conditions during early training, allowing the model to first learn clean pulse representations before being exposed to composite interference. MR-TAE-FULL-NP (no-phase curriculum) achieves NCC 0.8138 and SNR improvement 7.33 dB, improving on the phased curriculum in synthetic metrics while slightly degrading gNCC to 0.4128.

The IDWT decoder variant (MR-TAE-FULL-IDWT) achieves NCC 0.8037 and SNR improvement 6.89 dB under the no-phase curriculum. While the IDWT decoder achieves a comparable synthetic NCC, its gNCC of 0.2550 without fine-tuning is substantially lower than the linear decoder's 0.4366, suggesting that the IDWT decoder's frequency-structured output projection introduces additional distribution shift when applied to real-domain recordings whose noise characteristics differ from the synthetic training distribution.

### Deep Learning Baselines

All three deep learning baselines were trained for 50 epochs on the flat composite distribution without curriculum scheduling or multi-task supervision, providing a lower-bound reference consistent with prior literature. UNet1D_simple achieves the highest baseline NCC of 0.8016 and SNR improvement of 9.80 dB, but still lower than MR-TAE-FULL under the same flat training regime (NCC 0.8016 vs 0.8138) and without the segmentation capability. DnCNN1D achieves NCC 0.7393 and a competitive gNCC of 0.4717, the highest among the baselines on real-domain data. PureCNN1D achieves NCC 0.7223 with 0.21M parameters, offering the lowest computational cost at the expense of accuracy.

The critical distinction between MR-TAE and these baselines is not synthetic NCC alone: MR-TAE-FULL additionally delivers Dice 0.9015 discharge-type segmentation that none of the baselines can provide, and its gNCC under domain adaptation substantially exceeds all competitors.

### Classical Signal Processing Baselines

Among classical methods, Wavelet BayesShrink achieves the highest synthetic NCC (0.6578) and gNCC (0.3844), confirming that adaptive threshold selection provides meaningful advantage over fixed-threshold wavelet processing. The Wiener filter (NCC 0.5897) and Savitzky-Golay filter (NCC 0.0351) perform substantially worse, with Savitzky-Golay's near-zero NCC reflecting the catastrophic over-smoothing that destroys the sharp rise-time characteristics of PD pulses. The NoMix + Q.Lin fine-tuned variant of MR-TAE achieves gNCC 0.4535, exceeding BayesShrink by 17.9% without fine-tuning.

## Real-Domain Transfer and Efficiency

### Grounded Real-Domain NCC

The grounded real-domain NCC (gNCC) is the headline real-world performance metric, computed by evaluating model outputs against clean ground-truth waveforms from the Q.Lin real-recording dataset. Without domain adaptation, MR-TAE-FULL achieves gNCC 0.4366 and the LossB-IDWT variant achieves gNCC 0.5173. Following Q.Lin domain adaptation, the fine-tuned linear model achieves gNCC 0.7871 and the fine-tuned IDWT model achieves gNCC 0.7846, both substantially exceeding the BayesShrink reference.

The per-SNR breakdown of the fine-tuned model reveals gNCC 0.9133 at 0 dB and gNCC 0.9859 at +15 dB on real Q.Lin windows, demonstrating near-perfect morphological recovery at moderate to low noise levels following relatively lightweight domain adaptation. ### Computational Efficiency Analysis

Figure 4.6 presents the efficiency scatter plot of latency (batch size 1, in milliseconds) versus synthetic NCC, with bubble area proportional to parameter count. The Pareto frontier is traced from MWCNN-BiGRU (lightest, 1.31M parameters, 3.8 ms) through noSwin-noAttn (best speed-accuracy trade-off, 3.01M parameters, 8.8 ms) to MR-TAE-FULL (highest accuracy, 3.01M parameters, 40.1 ms). MR-TAE-FULL's 40.1 ms latency at batch size 1 is attributable primarily to the Swin Transformer's shifted-window attention computation, which dominates the bottleneck runtime.

The noSwin-noAttn configuration deserves particular attention from a deployment standpoint: at 8.8 ms it achieves NCC 0.7998 and gNCC 0.4171 while operating nearly five times faster. For applications where latency is a primary constraint and the marginal accuracy gain of the full Swin-Attention pathway is acceptable to trade off, noSwin-noAttn represents the preferred embedded deployment target.

## Explainability Analysis

LIME and SHAP are computed on hard windows at −15 dB SNR for all 13 ablation configurations and the IDWT decoder variants. Explainability analysis at the most challenging noise level ensures that the attribution results reflect the model's behaviour under the conditions where architectural choices matter most.

### LIME Analysis

On MR-TAE-FULL at −15 dB, LIME segment importance peaks at 0.2342 with a peak-to-mean ratio of 1.13, consistent with pulse-focused denoising in which attention concentrates on the mid-window time steps carrying the PD transients rather than on the uniform background noise regions. The moderate peak-to-mean ratio (1.13 vs the theoretical maximum of ~3-4 for a perfectly localised explanation) indicates that the model's denoising strategy is not purely pulse-triggered. It also applies global noise suppression across the full window but the systematic concentration of importance mass on the pulse region confirms that the model has learned a semantically correct denoising strategy.

The component importance ranking from LIME aligns quantitatively with the ablation NCC drops: wavelet encoder first (NCC drop 0.1688), multi-task head second (NCC drop 0.1509), BiGRU third (NCC drop 0.1427), Swin Transformer fourth (NCC drop 0.1359), and attention gate fifth (NCC drop 0.1223). This cross-method consistency, two independent evaluation frameworks (ablation NCC and LIME attribution) producing the same rank order provides strong evidence that the performance hierarchy reflects genuine architectural necessity rather than experimental artefact.

### SHAP Integrated-Gradients Analysis

SHAP integrated-gradients analysis yields a mean absolute attribution of 0.001405 across the input sample dimension. Attribution mass concentrates on mid-window samples carrying PD transients rather than being distributed uniformly across the background, confirming that the model has learned to locate and preserve the diagnostic pulse regions rather than applying a global smoothing operation. This localisation is diagnostically important: a model that applied uniform smoothing might achieve reasonable SNR improvement metrics by attenuating background noise but would simultaneously distort the pulse morphology on which fault classification depends.

## Summary of Results

Across all evaluation axes, the MR-TAE architecture demonstrates consistent and substantial advantages over both classical signal processing methods and simpler deep learning baselines. The five principal findings are:

1\. Wavelet pooling and the MTL segmentation head are the two indispensable components. Their removal causes the only sign reversals in the entire ablation (gNCC from +0.4366 to −0.1605 and −0.0337 respectively), confirming that lossless frequency decomposition and morphology-preserving multi-task supervision are architectural requirements for real-world generalisation.

2\. The NoMix curriculum achieves the best synthetic performance (NCC 0.8282, SNR improvement 9.64 dB), while MR-TAE-FULL phased curriculum provides the best balance of synthetic and real performance for general deployment.

3\. At extreme noise (−15 dB), MR-TAE-FULL achieves NCC 0.3492 versus BayesShrink's 0.1575, a relative improvement of 122%. This margin closes as SNR improves, with all models converging near NCC 0.95 at +15 dB.

4\. Domain adaptation to Q.Lin real recordings dramatically improves gNCC from 0.4366 to 0.7871 (linear decoder), achieving 0.9859 at +15 dB, near-perfect morphological recovery on unseen real measurements. Both fine-tuned variants (linear and IDWT decoder) exceed BayesShrink's fine-tuned equivalent.

5\. LIME and SHAP explainability analyses independently confirm the ablation component ranking (wavelet > MTL > BiGRU > Swin > Attention) and demonstrate that the model's denoising strategy is correctly localised to mid-window PD transient samples rather than applying indiscriminate global smoothing.

# Discussion

## Component Importance and Design Recommendations

The ablation experiment is designed as a controlled factorial study. Every configuration shares the training schedule, data seed, frozen test sets and evaluation pipeline, so performance differences are attributable to the toggled component alone.

The results establish a clear hierarchy of component importance. Wavelet pooling is the single most important component, with its removal causing the largest synthetic NCC drop and a collapse of grounded real NCC to negative values. This confirms that frequency-aware, lossless downsampling is the architectural foundation for robust PD denoising. Standard convolutional downsampling, as used in UNet-BiGRU-Swin (row 13), discards the high-frequency sub-bands that encode PD pulse rise times and oscillation frequencies.

The multi-task segmentation head is the second most critical component. Its removal produces the most severe real-domain failure, with grounded real NCC collapsing to -0.1605. This demonstrates that the segmentation constraint is not merely a convenience for downstream classification but a morphology-preservation regulariser that forces the encoder to retain the discriminative features of the PD pulse waveform. A model trained purely for signal reconstruction learns to suppress noise by smoothing, which removes the features required for real-world generalisation.

The counter-intuitive finding that removing both BiGRU and Swin together (row 7) costs almost nothing relative to the full model is an important practical insight. It suggests that the bottleneck's value lies in its capacity for sequence modelling in general, and that either BiGRU or Swin alone is sufficient to provide that capacity. For latency-constrained applications, MR-TAE-noSwin-noAttn (row 8) achieves equivalent NCC at 8.75 ms, making it the recommended lightweight variant.

## Discharge-Type Robustness

A model that achieves Dice 0.9015 across five discharge classes at SNR as low as -15 dB is preserving the pulse morphology that distinguishes corona from internal and surface discharges. This performance is directly enabled by the joint denoising and segmentation objective, as confirmed by the near-zero Dice of all configurations that remove the segmentation head.

The per-gap-size robustness of the grounded real evaluation further supports this conclusion. Q.Lin signals from all four gap sizes (1.0, 1.8, 2.0 and 2.5 mm) are included in the 35,000-window grounded test set, and the finetuned model achieves NCC above 0.98 at +15 dB across all gap geometries, demonstrating that denoising quality generalises across defect geometries and severity levels.

Practitioners deploying this model can therefore expect not only noise suppression but also reliable discharge-type identification on the denoised output, without any additional classification stage.

## Comparison with Deep Learning Baselines

The UNet1D_simple achieves NCC 0.8016 on synthetic data and SNR improvement 9.80 dB, which numerically exceeds MR-TAE-FULL on these metrics. However, this comparison is not equivalent: UNet1D_simple was trained 50 epochs on the flat composite distribution without curriculum scheduling or multi-task supervision. When MR-TAE is trained under equivalent no-curriculum conditions (linear no-phase), it achieves NCC 0.8138, and with the NoMix curriculum it reaches 0.8282. The critical distinction is that MR-TAE-FULL additionally provides Dice 0.9015 discharge-type segmentation that UNet1D_simple cannot offer. On the grounded real metric, MR-TAE-FULL (0.4366) exceeds UNet1D_simple (0.4213), and the domain-adapted MR-TAE variants (0.78-0.80) substantially outperform all 50-epoch baselines.

## Limitations

Training relies on synthetic supervision because clean real PD signals cannot be recorded under operational conditions. The Q.Lin dataset represents a single laboratory environment with one insulation type and a limited set of artificial defect geometries. WGAN-GP augmentation to better match the real noise distribution is specified in the pipeline but is left for future work. Where grounded real NCC is modest in the non-finetuned configurations, the result reflects a genuine domain-transfer limitation rather than a measurement artefact.

# Conclusion and Future Work

MR-TAE, a single unified multi-task autoencoder for AE-PD denoising, has been presented. The model combines frequency-aware MWCNN sampling with a sequential BiGRU and 1-D Swin-Transformer bottleneck, attention-gated skip connections and a dual-stream segmentation head. The full design space has been studied under a single grounded, SNR-stratified protocol spanning -15 to +15 dB on both synthetic and real Q.Lin data, with a domain-adaptation study that demonstrates real-world generalisability.

The key findings are as follows. On synthetic data, MR-TAE achieves mean NCC 0.7991 and SNR improvement 7.01 dB, exceeding BayesShrink by 4.28 dB. The model achieves Dice 0.9015 across five PD discharge types at -15 dB SNR. The noMTL ablation confirms that joint denoising and discharge-type localisation are mutually dependent: without the segmentation head, the denoised signal loses real-world morphology fidelity entirely. Following Q.Lin domain adaptation, grounded real NCC rises to 0.7871, a 104.8% improvement over BayesShrink and an 80% improvement over the non-adapted model. The IDWT decoder variant achieves these results at 2.92 M parameters, 0.09 M fewer than the linear variant, making it the recommended choice for resource-constrained deployment.

Future work includes four directions. First, WGAN-GP augmentation is planned to better match the real noise distribution. Second, self-supervised adaptation in the style of Noise2Void will be investigated to enable training directly on unlabelled field data. Third, multi-sensor fusion will be explored for PD source localisation. Fourth, edge deployment via pruning and INT8 quantisation is targeted for the NXP i.MX 8M Plus platform.
